item.title: Re: SCP-something: Man unable to communicate properly
item.content:encoded:
Of the new stuff you've added, I have to say that the end of the new interview might be the most compelling part. At its core, the emotionally compelling elements here are centered around SCPxx's struggle to communicate what it perceives as a terrifying threat. The actual threat may or may not exist, but the truly evocative lines in this come from SCPxx's frustration and desperation. I'd recommend leaning into that.

I'd also like to echo my previous recommendation to reconsider some of your redactions. As discussed in MalyceGraves' exceptional guide on the subject, the style you're utilizing here isn't the best way to communicate your plot.

item.title: Re: SCP-something: Man unable to communicate properly
item.content:encoded:
It's not blasphemy to ask questions! We can think of a story as a way of building up tension and stakes for the reader. The ending, in that conventional line of thinking, should be a way of relieving that tension in a way that leaves the reader. This can be a resolution of a mystery, the end of an emotional arc, or even a twist that casts the previous elements in a drastically different light.

At the moment, it seems like you're trying to relieve the tension in a bunch of different ways at once without committing to any of them. Since each of your endings are 'twists' that are mostly unconnected to each other, it seems like the article "zig-zags" between different hints without taking the time to relate them to the actual narrative. Does that make sense?

item.title: Re: SCP-something: Man unable to communicate properly
item.content:encoded:
Thanks for the advice! The food for thought was very nutritious.
I completely agree that there were some unnecessary redactions, and I've removed the extraneous ones.
I never meant to give the impression that the Foundation was hostile towards SCPxx, only that Dr Adam Pink was. I've made a few adjustments to make that point clearer.
As for the ending, I'll agree that there are several rather unconnected threads, and that there is no clear conclusion to the story. However (and I may be blaspheming with this statement), is that such a bad thing? My goal with the article is for the reader to feel drawn into the mystery, and to feel a level of compassion for the SCP. I think most of the article does a reasonable job of fostering that. The sideline with the missing husband, in my opinion, is reasonably unsettling if nothing else.
I should also mention that one of my goals for the article was to write it in such a way that the SCP might not be anomalous at all.
In any case, I don't doubt that I'll be making adjustments to the article for a while yet. Thank you for looking at it!

item.title: Re: SCP-something: Man unable to communicate properly
item.content:encoded:
Placeholder! Got summoned via PM to take a look-see. Will crit in a bit.

So sorry for the wait! This is pretty good for a first draft, but here are my critiques:

+ show block
– hide block

First off, I’d recommend looking through the Butterfly Squad Roster for a critter with experience in line-by-line/detailed crit or clinical tone. You’ve done pretty well overall, but there’s definitely some common first-draft mistakes in here. In particular, a lot of the redaction and expungement is reminiscent of Series I. For a more modern philosophy of elision, I’d recommend reading this exceptional guide from the esteemed MalyceGraves.

The animosity that the Foundation seems to display towards SCPxx also feels somewhat outdated. I say this with the caveat that the Foundation’s beliefs and practices are very much up to interpretation; however, the kind of animosity they display here against a relatively harmless anomaly doesn’t feel justified. If the Foundation isn’t being cruel to SCPxx, on the other hand, why would they allow a doctor to be in charge of its research despite actively doubting its nature?

I’m also not so sure what you’re trying to do with the ending. Instead of ending the narrative of them trying to figure out what SCPxx is actually saying, we have the original picture ending, the muttering ending, and the missing person ending, all of which are separate from each other. What do you want the reader to feel once they finish the article? In your opinion, what is the end of your narrative?


If you respond to this comment and would like me to see it, please send me a Wikidot PM, as I will not be notified otherwise.

item.title: Re: SCP-something: Man unable to communicate properly
item.content:encoded:
Note: Not a verified reviewer. Take my words with a grain of salt.

Hmm, this is pretty interesting! While there are many anomalies dealing with difficult communication, this one is certainly unique. The interview log really adds to it in my opinion.
There are a couple things here and there that could be refined. For example, "Foundation" should be written with a capitalized F. Also, this part:

-Pretend to sing opera for two minutes and thirty-eight seconds. SCPxx gave such a good performance that several observers thought that they had gone deaf when they couldn’t hear any singing.

The "such a good performance" kind of breaks the clinical tone. You could just phrase it like "Several observers believed they had gone deaf, although they reported hearing no singing" or something like that.

This all being said, I'm not a pro reviewer, so I suggest you ask critique from people that know how to do it better. I wish you the best of luck with your writing!
